title: Spelling Test Fixes
story: A primary-school teacher scores each word on a spelling test by "fixes": the smallest number of single-letter fixes that turn the child's attempt into the correct word. A fix adds one letter, removes one letter, or changes one letter into another.
She wants a program to work out the score.
task: Write fewestFixes(attempt, word). Return the smallest number of fixes that turn attempt into word, where each fix inserts one letter anywhere, deletes one letter, or replaces one letter with a different letter.
If the strings are equal, return 0. Either string may be empty.
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase letters a to z.

examples.explanation: Change the i to e and the e after it to i: 2 fixes. There is no 1-fix answer, because the strings differ in two positions and have the same length, so one insert or delete cannot help.
Keep the n, the i and the t. Add a g and an h before the t, then remove the final e. That is 3 fixes, and no shorter list of fixes works.

hints: Compare frend and friend position by position. How many positions differ, and how many fixes does it really take?

One missing letter shifts everything after it, so positions cannot be fixed independently. Look at the last letters instead. If they are equal, they need no fix: drop both and score the rest. If not, the last fix involves them.

If the last letters differ, there are three options: replace the attempt's last letter (both shrink by one), delete it (attempt shrinks), or insert the word's last letter (word shrinks). Take the cheapest and add 1.

Let fix[i][j] be the score for the first i letters of attempt and the first j of word. The first row is j (insert everything), the first column is i (delete everything). Fill row by row: diagonal if the letters match, else 1 + min(diagonal, above, left).
bruteForce: Run a breadth-first search over every string reachable in 1 fix, then in 2 fixes, and so on. Each string has hundreds of neighbours, so after a few levels there are billions of strings.
A recursive last-letter rule is smaller but still exponential, because it reaches the same pair of prefixes along many paths. For 500-letter strings you need a table.

js: * @return {number} fewest single-letter inserts, deletes or replacements
py: def fewest_fixes(attempt: str, word: str) -> int:

tests.note: defeats counting a replace as delete + insert

js: // prev[j] = fixes for the previous prefix of attempt and word[0..j)
let prev = Array.from({ length: m + 1 }, (_, j) => j); // empty attempt: insert j letters
const cur = [i]; // empty word: delete i letters
if (attempt[i - 1] === word[j - 1]) cur[j] = prev[j - 1]; // last letters match
py: # prev[j] = fixes for the previous prefix of attempt and word[:j]
prev = list(range(m + 1))  # empty attempt: insert j letters
cur = [i] + [0] * m  # empty word: delete i letters
walkthrough: Work on prefixes and look at the last letters. If they match, keep them for free. If not, the cheapest plan ends with one of three fixes: replace (both shrink), delete (the attempt shrinks) or insert (the word shrinks). Each table cell holds the score for one pair of prefixes.
Trace "cut" into "cat". Rows are prefixes of the attempt, columns prefixes of the word:
• Row "u", column "a": u ≠ a, so 1 + min(0, 1, 1) = 1, the replace u → a.
The answer, bottom-right, is 1. The edges are the base cases: one delete per letter to reach the empty string, one insert per letter to build from nothing.
solution.timeWhy: Each of the (n + 1) × (m + 1) cells takes constant time.
solution.spaceWhy: Only the previous row and the current row are kept.
solution.takeaway: To compare two strings with edits, build a table over pairs of prefixes. A match copies the diagonal; otherwise take 1 plus the cheapest of the three neighbours, one per kind of edit. Spell checkers, diff tools and DNA alignment all use this table.
